passage:
Dilnaz,

You asked me last night, crying, why I always "disappear." I couldn't answer then. I'm trying now, on paper, where my voice doesn't lock up.

When you start with "we need to talk" and then "you never" and "why don't you," something in my chest goes tight and loud, like a pressure cooker. I can't find words fast enough. Anything I say feels like it'll make it worse. So I go quiet. I put my earphones in. Yesterday I walked out and sat on the hostel terrace for an hour.

In my head, I'm stopping a fight. I honestly thought I was protecting us.

But I saw your face when I came back. You looked like I'd left you at a station. I didn't know it felt like that for you.

I don't know how to fix it yet. I just didn't want you to think I don't care.

Danish

qa.q: Where did Danish sit for an hour after walking out?
qa.a: Danish sat on the hostel terrace for an hour.

qa.q: What does Danish feel when Dilnaz starts with 'we need to talk'?
qa.a: Danish feels overwhelmed, a tight, loud pressure in the chest, and can't find words, so going quiet feels like the only safe option.

qa.q: What could Danish try instead of putting in earphones or leaving?
qa.a: Danish could say, 'I'm overwhelmed, give me a little time and I'll come back to this,' so the pause doesn't feel like abandonment.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz experience Danish going quiet?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels abandoned and hurt, as if left at a station, rather than seeing it as avoiding a fight.

grounding: A letter shows one partner flooding under criticism and withdrawing to avoid a fight, while the other experiences it as abandonment.

passage:
Samir, you think your Hansa Nani was always this calm? Let me tell you about the year before I married your Nana.

I was twenty, he was twenty-two, and we wrote letters because the phone was in the neighbour's house. When he stopped writing for two weeks, I was sure he'd changed his mind.

So I wrote more. Six pages. Then ten. I asked why he was cold, whether there was another girl, why he didn't care. When he replied with three short lines, I cried and wrote twelve pages back, all accusation.

Years later he told me each long letter made him want to hide under the bed. And every short reply made me write longer. We were both sure the other had started it.

What stopped it? I finally took the bus to his town and just sat with him, no speeches. That was the turning point.

qa.q: How many pages was the letter Hansa wrote back after the three-line reply?
qa.a: She wrote twelve pages back.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when the letters stopped for two weeks?
qa.a: She felt afraid that he had changed his mind, and the fear pushed her to write longer, more accusing letters.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Taking the bus to sit with him without speeches; it broke the loop because there was no pressure for him to retreat from.

qa.q: How might the young Nana have felt receiving the ten- and twelve-page letters?
qa.a: He likely felt overwhelmed and accused, wanting to hide, which made him write even less.

grounding: An elder recalls how silence fed her fear, so she pushed harder, and how her partner retreated further, each sure the other started it.

subtype: Stage 5: Seeing the loop, not the villain [Response]
passage:
Sunday

Sarika and I had the best talk we've had in months. Not a fight. A talk.

It happened on the college steps after the play. We were both tired and in a good mood, and she said, "Can I say something without us fighting?"

She said: "When you go quiet, I get scared, so I push." I said: "And when you push, I panic, so I go quieter." We both laughed, because it was so obvious once it was out loud. Like a see-saw.

Then she said something I've been thinking about all evening: "Maybe it's not you or me. It's the see-saw."

So we gave it a name. When it starts, either of us can just say "see-saw," and we stop and check.

I feel lighter tonight than in weeks.

Asif

qa.q: Where did Asif and Sarika have their talk?
qa.a: They talked on the college steps after the play.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling at the end of the evening?
qa.a: Asif felt lighter and relieved, and hopeful that naming the pattern could help.

qa.q: Why is naming the pattern 'see-saw' a useful step?
qa.a: It turns the cycle into the problem instead of each other, and gives both a quick, neutral way to stop and check when it starts.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when she asked to speak without fighting?
qa.a: Sarika was probably hopeful but a little nervous, wanting to share her fear without setting off another round.

grounding: In a calm moment two partners name their pursue-withdraw pattern together and treat the cycle, not each other, as the enemy.

subtype: Stage 6: Softer ask and staying present [Response]
passage:
Rashmi, you asked how your Vijay Dada and I have lasted fifty years. Sit, I'll tell you the real answer.

When we were first married, I was twenty-two and a clam. If your Dadi raised her voice, I shut like a door. And she, poor thing, would get louder: "You never talk to me! You don't care!"

One night she didn't shout. She sat on the bed and said, very quietly, "I miss you. I'm scared we're becoming strangers." I nearly cried.

I said, "I go quiet because I get overwhelmed. Give me twenty minutes, and I'll come back. I promise."

I walked around the block. Twenty minutes later, I was back. We talked till two in the morning.

From then on, she said the soft thing instead of the sharp thing, and I always came back. That's the whole secret, beta.

qa.q: How long did Vijay ask for before coming back?
qa.a: He asked for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when Dadi said she missed him and was scared?
qa.a: He felt deeply moved, nearly crying, because the soft words reached him where the shouting hadn't.

qa.q: What was the choice inside the story that changed their pattern?
qa.a: Dadi spoke her fear instead of criticism, and Vijay named his need for a short break and actually came back, so trust could grow.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Vijay returned after twenty minutes?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and valued, seeing that his break wasn't a retreat from her.

grounding: An elder recalls how a softer ask replaced criticism and a promised, kept return replaced silence.

subtype: Stage 1: Work stress and quiet distance [Receiver]
passage:
The hospital canteen was nearly empty at 10 p.m. when Ishita found Vijay at the corner table, still in his scrubs after a fourteen-hour shift.

"I brought you a dosa," she said, sitting across from him. "Guess what happened at my office today—"

"Mm." He nodded, eyes on his tea.

She tried again. "My manager finally said yes to the Pune trip."

"That's good." He rubbed his forehead. He hadn't looked up.

Ishita put down her fork. This was the fourth evening like this. In her head, a small voice said: He doesn't even want me here anymore.

Vijay, for his part, was thinking only that his ears were ringing from the ward and that silence felt like the kindest thing in the world. He had no idea she was reading his quiet as a verdict on her.

qa.q: How long was Vijay's shift?
qa.a: His shift was fourteen hours.

qa.q: What is Ishita worried about as she puts down her fork?
qa.a: She is hurt and worried that Vijay no longer wants her around, reading his flat evenings as rejection.

qa.q: What could each of them try to avoid this misunderstanding?
qa.a: Vijay could say, 'I'm wiped out, it's not you, I just need quiet,' and Ishita could ask directly instead of guessing.

qa.q: How does Vijay experience the evening differently from Ishita?
qa.a: Vijay simply feels exhausted and craves silence, with no intention of rejecting her and no idea how she reads it.

grounding: A worn-out partner wants only quiet after a demanding job, and the other reads the flat evenings as a sign she no longer matters.

passage:
Couples counselling, session note, week 2.

Indu and Pankaj, married eighteen months. Indu described the past month in detail, and it was clear she has been reaching out many times a day in small ways.

Examples she gave: sending Pankaj a funny video at work, asking about his cricket team, resting her hand on his shoulder while he cooked. Most went unanswered. He admits he often didn't notice.

Indu said each missed moment "stings a little, like a paper cut." After a few weeks, she said, she stopped joking and started saying, "You never listen to me." She was surprised to hear herself.

Pankaj looked genuinely startled to learn the videos had meant anything.

Plan agreed: for one week, each will notice and respond to one small reach from the other per day. We will review next Tuesday.

qa.q: How long have Indu and Pankaj been married?
qa.a: They have been married eighteen months.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when her small reaches were missed?
qa.a: Indu felt a small sting each time, like a paper cut, and over weeks her hurt turned into complaints.

qa.q: Why is the plan to answer one small reach a day a wise step?
qa.a: It makes the small bids visible and gives Indu some response, before her frustration grows into bigger complaints.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel learning that the videos mattered to Indu?
qa.a: Pankaj seems startled and perhaps a little guilty, realising he missed something important without meaning to.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a partner making small bids for attention, feeling stung when they are missed, until requests become complaints.

passage:
Yusuf,

I'm writing this because when we talk I go blank, and then I do the thing you hate.

On Tuesday you said, "You're never here, even when you're here." You weren't wrong. But what I felt in that moment wasn't anger. It was: I'm failing at work, and now I'm failing at home too.

So I did what I always do. I said I had a report to finish and stayed at the laptop till one. Wednesday I worked late on purpose. Last night I scrolled for two hours in bed, next to you.

I think the phone and the office are where I hide from that feeling. If I'm not with you, I can't let you down in person.

I know it looks like I don't care. It's the opposite, which makes it stupid.

I don't want to keep hiding.

Chinmay

qa.q: What did Yusuf say to Chinmay on Tuesday?
qa.a: Yusuf said, "You're never here, even when you're here."

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel when Yusuf said that?
qa.a: Chinmay felt inadequate, like a failure at both work and home, which led to shutting down and hiding in work and the phone.

qa.q: What could Chinmay try instead of staying at the laptop?
qa.a: Chinmay could name the feeling out loud, for example 'I feel like I'm failing,' and ask for a moment, rather than retreating into work.

qa.q: How might Yusuf be affected by Chinmay's late nights and scrolling?
qa.a: Yusuf likely feels lonely and ignored, reading the retreat as not caring, when it comes from fear of letting Yusuf down.

grounding: A letter shows a partner who hears criticism, feels inadequate and retreats into work and the phone to avoid that feeling.

passage:
Looking back at that winter, I can see how both of us were keeping score. I'm Jasleen, and I'll tell my side first, since that's the side I lived in.

I felt invisible. Charan came home, ate, disappeared into his laptop. I'd plan Sunday outings and he'd say he was tired. I started keeping a list in my head: I cooked, I planned, I asked. He did nothing.

Months later he told me his list. He said he felt like nothing he did was right. He'd fix the geyser and I'd point out the tap. He'd come home early and I'd say it was too late. In his story, he was the one trying, and I was the one who was never satisfied.

The worst part is that we both stopped being kind in small ways. No tea brought unasked. No "how was your day" that meant it. Just two scorekeepers.

qa.q: What did Charan fix, according to his list?
qa.a: Charan fixed the geyser.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling that winter?
qa.a: Jasleen felt lonely and invisible, resentful that Charan seemed to do nothing.

qa.q: What could have interrupted the scorekeeping earlier?
qa.a: Either of them could have shared their private list calmly, asking 'what does it feel like for you?', or brought in a trusted friend or counsellor to hear both sides.

qa.q: How did Charan experience the same winter?
qa.a: Charan felt nagged and never good enough, sure he was the one trying while Jasleen was never satisfied.

grounding: A reflective account shows both partners keeping private stories in which they are the one trying, while kindness toward each other thins.

passage:
Friday: Keerthana met Jahnavi for coffee. Jahnavi talked for an hour about Nikhil: always tired, never listening, "like living with a wall." Keerthana noticed her friend's hands shaking around the cup. She didn't hear cruelty in the story. She heard loneliness.

Sunday: Nikhil came to Keerthana's flat to return a borrowed drill and ended up staying for tea. He said, flatly, "Nothing I do is enough for her." Then he stared at the floor. Keerthana thought: he sounds hurt, not cold.

Wednesday: Keerthana called each of them. To Jahnavi she said, "I don't think he's pulling away because he doesn't care. He sounds like he's drowning." To Nikhil: "She's not attacking you. She misses you." She refused to say who was right. That night Jahnavi texted her: "We actually talked. Thank you."

qa.q: What did Nikhil come to return?
qa.a: He came to return a borrowed drill.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she listened to each of them?
qa.a: Keerthana felt concerned and caring, seeing both friends as lonely and hurt rather than uncaring.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's approach help without making things worse?
qa.a: Keerthana shared with each what the other seemed to feel and refused to take sides, so neither felt judged and both could see the other differently.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Nikhil after Keerthana's call?
qa.a: Jahnavi may begin to see Nikhil as overwhelmed rather than cold, which made it possible for them to really talk.

grounding: Across several days a close friend notices both partners are lonely and hurt, gently tells each partner what the other is feeling and takes no side.

subtype: Stage 6: Scheduled closeness and honest limits [Response]
passage:
Monday: Hemant came home at nine, dropped his bag and said nothing. Dhruv, who'd been waiting all evening to talk, felt the familiar panic rise. But this time Hemant said it out loud: "I'm spent. Give me an hour, then I'm yours." Dhruv set a timer on his phone, half-annoyed, half-hopeful.

Thursday: At 10:05 the timer rang. Hemant came out of the shower, sat on the balcony next to Dhruv and asked, "Okay. Tell me about your day." Dhruv noticed he felt calmer waiting, because he knew when Hemant would come.

The following Sunday: They kept the new standing plan: Sunday breakfast, no phones, unhurried. Hemant admitted he'd stopped feeling guilty for needing that hour. Dhruv said he'd stopped counting the hours Hemant was quiet.

qa.q: What did Hemant say when he came home on Monday?
qa.a: He said, "I'm spent. Give me an hour, then I'm yours."

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he set the timer on Monday?
qa.a: Dhruv felt half-annoyed and half-hopeful, still used to panicking when Hemant went quiet.

qa.q: Why do the hour and the Sunday breakfast work together?
qa.a: The hour gives Hemant space without guilt, and the regular breakfast gives Dhruv a predictable time for closeness.

qa.q: How does Hemant feel about needing time alone after the change?
qa.a: Hemant has stopped feeling guilty for needing the hour, because it now comes with a clear promise to return.

grounding: Across more than a week two partners set a regular unhurried time and a clear 'give me an hour' signal, giving predictability and space.
